t: Reverse Words With Same Vowel Count
o: We split the string into words, count vowels in the first word, and for every subsequent word with the same vowel count we output its reverse; all other words pass through unchanged. In example 1, "cat" has 1 vowel so "and" (1 vowel) becomes "dna", while "mice" (2 vowels) stays. In example 2, "book" has 2 vowels, so only "nice" is reversed to "ecin". With $n \le 10^5$, any linear scan over the characters works — no fancy data structures are needed.
k: Count vowels per word with a simple helper; a single pass over each character suffices.
The first word is never reversed regardless of its own vowel count.
Reversing can be done via slicing/reverse iterators or by walking the word backwards while building the answer.

a.i: Split the string on spaces into words, compute the vowel count of the first word as the target, then rebuild the result: keep the first word as-is and reverse every later word whose vowel count equals the target. This directly mirrors the problem statement and runs in linear time since each character is visited a constant number of times.
s: Split s into a list of words.
Count vowels in words[0] to get target count k.
For each later word, append its reverse if its vowel count equals k, else append it unchanged.
Join with single spaces and return.
a.t: O(n) — splitting, counting, and reversing each touch every character a constant number of times.
a.sp: O(n) — storing the split words and the result string.

a.i: Avoid materializing a word list: scan the string once, tracking the start of the current word. When a word ends, decide whether to copy it forward or backwards using two pointers. The first completed word sets the target vowel count and is always copied forward. This keeps memory to just the output buffer.
s: Initialize target = -1, i = 0, and an empty result builder.
For each word [i, j): if target is unset, set target = vowelCount(word) and copy forward; else copy forward if counts differ, backwards if equal.
Copy characters one by one into the result, appending a space before each word except the first.
Advance i past the word and repeat until the end of s.
a.t: O(n) — each character is examined during counting and copied exactly once into the result.
a.sp: O(n) — only the output buffer beyond O(1) extra state.

w: Use Approach 1 in an interview: it's the clearest and still optimal at $O(n)$; mention Approach 2 as a memory-conscious variant that avoids splitting. Pitfalls: forgetting that the first word is never reversed even if it matches itself; off-by-one errors when reversing with manual index loops; assuming multiple/leading/trailing spaces (constraints guarantee single spaces). Edge cases: a single-word string returns unchanged; words like "aeiou" (5 vowels) vs "bcdfg" (0 vowels). Follow-ups: handle arbitrary whitespace, do it in-place for mutable strings, or stream the answer without storing all words.
